**(B)** 1 : 2 : 1

In *Mirabilis jalapa* a red (RR) × white (rr) cross gives pink (Rr) F1 plants, and selfing them gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white in F2. Because the heterozygote shows its own intermediate colour, the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, instead of the 3 : 1 seen with complete dominance.

**(B)** nine

In a dihybrid cross each gene gives three genotypes in F2 (for example RR, Rr, rr and YY, Yy, yy), so the two genes together give 3 × 3 = 9 different genotypes among the 16 combinations of the Punnett square. Sixteen is the number of boxes, not of distinct genotypes, and four is the number of phenotypes.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives nine F2 genotypes in the ratio 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1.]

**(D)** test cross

Crossing an individual of unknown genotype with the homozygous recessive is a test cross: all dominant offspring show it is homozygous, while a 1 : 1 ratio shows it is heterozygous. A back cross is a cross of F1 with either parent, which need not be the recessive one, so it does not by itself test the genotype.

**(A)** incomplete dominance

In incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, so each genotype has its own phenotype and the F2 phenotypic ratio (1 red : 2 pink : 1 white) is the same as the genotypic ratio (1 : 2 : 1). With complete dominance the phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1 against a genotypic 1 : 2 : 1.

**(B)** Acrocentric

An acrocentric (J-shaped) chromosome has its centromere near one end, giving one very short arm and one long arm. In a telocentric chromosome the centromere is right at the end, in a metacentric it is in the middle, and in a submetacentric it is slightly away from the middle.

[Note: the chapter names the four types but does not state each centromere position; standard biology gives these positions.]

**(A)** Sutton and Boveri

Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri (1903) noticed that chromosomes behave during meiosis just as Mendel's factors do, and proposed that chromosomes carry the genes. Watson and Crick proposed the double helix model of DNA, while Miller and Urey, and Oparin and Haldane, are associated with the origin of life.

**(D)** p and s

Genes that lie far apart on a chromosome are loosely linked, because crossing over is more likely to occur somewhere between them, so they show more recombination. Of the pairs given, p and s are separated by two other genes, while the other pairs are neighbours, so p and s are least likely to be inherited together.

As printed, two pairs are mismatched, so no single answer is correct.

Down's syndrome is trisomy 21, with 47 chromosomes, so its formula is 45 + XY (or 45 + XX), not 44 + XY; a normal female is 44 + XX, not 44 + XXX. Turner's syndrome (44 + XO) and Klinefelter's syndrome (44 + XXY) are both correctly matched. The pair intended as the answer is most likely the normal female, but the Down's syndrome pair is equally wrong as printed.

**(A)** 0%

A son receives his X chromosome from his mother and his Y from his father. The mother here is homozygous normal (\(\text{X}^{\text{C}}\text{X}^{\text{C}}\)), so every son is \(\text{X}^{\text{C}}\text{Y}\) with normal vision; the father's \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) goes only to his daughters, who become carriers.
